extracted.intended_audience: Korean patent examiners and patent applicants (KIPO context)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for assessing novelty, public availability, and claim interpretation under the Korean Patent Act (Article 29 and related provisions), including handling of printed and electronic publications and principles for defining claimed inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be industrially applicable to be patentable; marketable or tradable subject matter is considered industrially applicable. Inventions used only for research or experimental purposes may be regarded as industrially inapplicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An invention is considered industrially applicable if it can be used in industry now or in the future. It is not sufficient that it works only in theory; inventions that cannot be implemented/practiced are not industrially applicable (example: covering the whole earth with UV-absorbing film is not implementable). The principle allows future applicability but does not extend applicability merely because technology may gradually advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventions that cannot be implemented
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention cannot be implemented or practiced (even if it works in theory), it is not considered industrially applicable and thus not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete implementability is required; speculative or physically impossible schemes are excluded (example given of impractical global-scale UV film).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty exclusion — prior public knowledge or working (Patent Act Article 29(1)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions publicly known or worked within or outside the Republic of Korea before filing are not novel and thus not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase was expanded to include knowledge/work outside Korea (applies to applications filed on/after 2006-10-01). Time of 'prior to filing' is the exact filing time (hour/minute) converted to Korean time. 'Unspecified persons' means the general public without secrecy obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty exclusion — inventions described in a distributed publication (Patent Act Article 29(1)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions described in a publication distributed in Korea or abroad, or published through electronic telecommunication lines as prescribed by Presidential Decree, before filing are not novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes printed documents, drawings, photographs duplicated for public disclosure; distribution means placed so unspecified persons can see/read it (actual access by a particular person not required). Patent gazettes on microfilm/CD-ROM and non-patent documents on similar media are considered distributed publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'publicly known invention'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A publicly known invention' means an invention the contents of which were known to an unspecified person without obligation of secrecy in Korea or a foreign country prior to filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time of prior knowledge is the exact filing time. 'Unspecified persons' refers to the general public with no duty of secrecy. Example: an unpublished application is not prior art under Article 29(1)(2) unless made available for public inspection after registration (then may be prior art under Article 20(1)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'publicly worked invention'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A publicly worked invention' means an invention which has been worked under conditions where the invention's contents are or can potentially be publicly known in Korea or abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being 'public' means no longer secret. If only a small inner part remains secret but the invention as worked is publicly observable/understandable by a skilled person, it's publicly worked. Potential public working includes situations where inner parts could be observed or explained to visitors and such access is not refused by the plant. Examples illustrate observation of manufacturing processes at exposed plants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributed publication — definition and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'publication' is a document, drawing or similar medium duplicated to disclose contents to the public by distribution; 'distribution' means placing the publication so unspecified persons can read or see it (actual access not required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media such as microfilm, CD-ROM, floppy discs, slides, presentations, etc., produced to make content available to the public are distributed publications. Catalogues published are presumed distributed as soon as published unless strong evidence to the contrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumptions for time of distribution/publication
rubrics_metrics.description: When publication time is indicated only partially or not at all, presumptions are applied: year-only → last day of year; month+year → last day of month; full date → that date. If no date, foreign distribution date presumed based on normal transit time to Korea, derivative publications use derivative's date; second editions use first edition date if contents accord; other appropriate information may be used to presume date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete example: catalogues are socially accepted as distributed upon publication; court decision cited for presumption that published catalogues are distributed before filing if evidence shows access in-country before filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention described in a publication — 'essentially described' standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is 'described in a publication' if it is identified by matters described or 'essentially described' (i.e., directly derivable from described matters considering common general knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a device to be 'described', at least the structure must be described; a mere photograph of an external appearance of an internal-featured device may not suffice. Example: photograph-only exhibits may not describe internal technical features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public availability via electronic telecommunication lines (Internet etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologies published over the Internet/electronic telecommunication lines can be prior art if the date and contents are entitled to public trust and, as prescribed, are treated the same as printed publications for Article 29(1)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internet disclosures need reliable proof of posting date and content because internet content can change. Provision distinguishes publications by designated telecommunication lines (per Presidential Decree) which can be cited as Article 29(1)(2) prior art; others may be prior art as publicly known under Article 29(1)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for electronic publications to be cited as prior art (Article 29(1)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: To cite an invention made available via electronic telecommunication lines as prior art under Article 29(1)(2), the information must be 'available to the public' via such lines and (for certain status) published by entities designated by Presidential Decree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key elements: (1) telecommunication lines include public bulletin boards, e-mail groups, internet; (2) 'available to the public' means accessible to unspecified persons and does not require actual access; (3) access restricted to specific persons (not public) is not 'available to the public'; (4) for Article 29(1)(2) status, the publishing entity must be designated (governments, national/public universities, national/public research institutes, corporations designated/publicly notified by KIPO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of 'telecommunication lines' for prior-art purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Telecommunication lines include wired/wireless/optic/other electromagnetic transmission/reception of code, words, sound or image; they encompass public bulletin boards, e-mail groups and future electronic methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media like CD-ROMs/diskettes are NOT considered telecommunication-line publications but are 'distributed publications'. Telecommunication lines need not be physical lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designated entities whose web publications are automatically reliable prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications on web sites owned by entities designated under the Presidential Decree are treated as reliable prior art under Article 29(1)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of designated entities: (i) governments/local governments/foreign governments/international organizations (UN, WIPO, WTO, EPO, ARIPO, OAPI, etc.), (ii) national/public universities under Higher Education Act, (iii) national/public research institutes, (iv) corporations designated and publicly notified by the Commissioner of KIPO (e.g., KIPA, Korea Institute of Patent Information). Publications on such sites can be cited without further verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding and proving time/content of electronic publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must determine time of publication and content of information retrieved from electronic telecommunication lines; if time/content are found in lines under Article 1bis Enforcement Decree, the examiner can cite without extra verification. If not, examiner must convince that posting was before filing through additional searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time of publication on electronic lines is the time the content was posted. If examiner cites such content, they must list the source and the time of publication. Applicants may argue against the examiner's recognition of time/content. If time cannot be found, the examiner may still cite after confirming posted-before-filing via additional searches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of citation for electronic prior art (bibliographic requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing electronic technical information, examiners should list bibliographic items (author, title, publication name, pages/drawings/graphs) in the order and format compliant with WIPO ST.14, insofar as known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a cited document is a patent published on the Internet, the examiner may describe it in the same way as patent official gazettes (e.g., CD-ROM form) without needing to state search date and web address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of hyperlinked other web-sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Web sites hyperlinked from web-sites covered by the Presidential Decree are not automatically reliable prior art under Article 1bis Enforcement Decree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperlinked sites' credibility of publication time cannot be guaranteed; therefore examiners should not treat them as automatically reliable prior art without independent verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference in status between designated electronic lines and other electronic lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions publicly known via electronic lines designated under Article 1bis Enforcement Decree have different evidentiary status (reliable prior art under Article 29(1)(2)) than those known via other electronic lines (which may be prior art only as publicly known under Article 29(1)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For designated lines, examiners can cite without more searches; for other lines, examiners must confirm posting date and content. A web-site restricted to a specific area (e.g., accessible only within a certain foreign college) may still be considered publicly known in the foreign country and thus prior art under Article 29(1)(1) but not under 29(1)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the identity of claimed inventions (novelty assessment procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is assessed by determining whether each claimed invention falls under inventions excluded by Article 29(1)(1)–(2). If it does, it's not novel; if not, it's novel. Each claim must be considered separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner shall judge novelty per claim. Claims must describe the subject matter for which protection is sought (Article 42(4)), so identity of invention is determined by the matters described in the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: General principles for defining inventions disclosed in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When claim language is clear, the claimed invention is defined as stated in the claim. Terminology in claims is given its general meaning in the technical field unless a specific meaning is explicitly defined in the description. Interpretation should be objective and reasonable considering common general knowledge at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should avoid narrowing interpretation by referencing detailed description/embodiments. If subject matter appears only in description/drawings and not in claims, the examiner should not treat it as claimed. Detailed description/drawings may be used to understand claims but not to add matter not in claims. Examples: 'cream' in claims should not be limited to a particular embodiment; drawings' rotation directions should not limit claims if not in claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant-defined terms / specific definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant specifically defines a term in the detailed description so that it clearly differs from the general meaning, that specific definition will be used to interpret the term in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely describing the specific concept of a term in the description does not automatically constitute a binding specific definition unless clearly intended. A term should be interpreted consistently across the specification; specific definitions in the description override general technical meaning when clearly stated (Supreme Court cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling obscure or unclear claim terms
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim term is obscure/unclear, the examiner should examine whether the claimed invention can be grasped in view of the detailed description, drawings and common general knowledge at filing; if it can, the examiner may notify refusal reasons on both lack of description and novelty together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim remains unclear even after consulting description/drawings/general knowledge, novelty examination is not conducted and a refusal for deficiency in specification is notified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting claims that specify products by function/characteristic/property
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim specifies a product by its function, property or characteristic, it should generally be construed to cover every product that has that function/characteristic, unless the expression is specifically defined otherwise in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take common general technical knowledge into account; however, in some cases a function/characteristic expression should not be construed broadly if context dictates. Example: 'means to selectively join plastic materials' would not apply to materials (e.g., magnetics) that are difficult to join with plastic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting use-limited claims (product-by-use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim limits a product by its use, the claim should be interpreted as covering a product specially suitable for the disclosed use, considering specification, drawings and common general knowledge at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A product that meets all technical characteristics but is not appropriate for the claimed use (or requires conversion) should not be regarded as the claimed product. If the product is not suitable for the use, the use-limitation may have no effect on defining the claimed invention and thus may not help preserve novelty. Example: a 'crane hook' is distinct from 'fishing hooks' even if both are hooks, because size/strength suit specific uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims (product defined by manufacturing process)
rubrics_metrics.description: A product claim that defines the product by its manufacturing process should, in principle, be construed as claiming the product per se; novelty/inventive step are determined by comparing the claimed product itself with prior art unless there is a special reason in the claim description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special reasons to accept process-limited product claims are extremely exceptional (e.g., when it's greatly difficult to define the product otherwise). If an identical product can be obtained by a different process, the claimed product is not novel.
